72T5smavl9ONfOwI0gHf1A.title: You're Dead

s.t: Norma Tanega meant ‘You’re Dead’ as a sarcastic indictment of the competition and consumerism that had engulfed New York’s folk scene.
s.src: Bleeding Cool: How You’re Dead became the franchise theme
s.q: The album would also include 'You're Dead,' which was meant as her sarcastic indictment of the competition and consumerism that had engulfed the New York folk scene.

s.t: Decades after Norma Tanega recorded it, ‘You’re Dead’ opened the vampire film What We Do in the Shadows; Taika Waititi and Jemaine Clement tracked her down for permission.
s.src: Bleeding Cool: How You’re Dead became the franchise theme
s.q: Waititi and Clement tracked down Tanega, who granted permission to use her song for the film and TV.

s.t: Once Norma Tanega’s ‘You’re Dead’ became the What We Do in the Shadows theme, Warner Music released a collection of her early recordings, In the Shadows, in 2019.
s.q: That same year, Warner Music released the collection In the Shadows comprising some of her early solo recordings after renewed interest in her music from its use on the  What We Do in the Shadows TV series.

f.t: Producer Herb Bernstein, then working with Tina Turner and Lesley Gore, tried to brush her off at their first meeting, then ‘flipped’ and thought she was fantastic.
f.src: Bandcamp Daily: Norma Tanega’s Unconventional Music Pushed the Boundaries of 1960s Folk
f.q: Bernstein, who at the time was producing big acts like Tina Turner and Lesley Gore, “To be honest with you, I tried to brush her off!” “I flipped. I thought she was fantastic.”

f.t: Her hit ‘Walkin’ My Cat Named Dog’ came from her New York apartment building banning dogs: she kept a cat instead, named it Dog and took it for walks.
f.q: Tanega's impetus for the song came from living in a New York City apartment building that did not allow dogs; instead she owned a cat which she named "Dog" and took for walks.

f.t: As the only woman on a North American tour with Gene Pitney, she was first backed by members of the Outsiders, who were replaced by session musicians because they couldn’t follow her idiosyncratic music.
f.q: a slot as the only woman on a North American tour with Gene Pitney, Bobby Goldsboro, Chad and Jeremy and The McCoys. During the tour, Tanega was initially backed by members of the Outsiders. Since they were unable to follow Tanega's more idiosyncratic music, the Outsiders were later replaced by session musicians

f.t: She lived with Dusty Springfield for five years, and Springfield recorded many of her songs, often as B-sides; she went uncredited on many of their collaborations.
f.q: Many of Tanega's songs appeared as non-album B-sides to Springfield's singles. ... Tanega also went uncredited for many of her collaborations with Springfield

f.t: In the 1980s she played in the Ceramic Ensemble, a group performing on handmade earthenware instruments made by ceramics professor Brian Ransom.
f.q: In the 1980s, she was a member of Scripps ceramics professor Brian Ransom's Ceramic Ensemble, a group that played Ransom's handmade earthenware instruments.

nf.q: which was written as a sarcastic statement about her struggles in New York's competitive music scene, was used in the opening credits of the New Zealand vampire comedy film What We Do in the Shadows
